Features

The intelligence other backup tools leave out.

Borg, restic and Time Machine are excellent vaults. BackDown adds the layer that tells you what you're actually storing.

Works todayIn developmentPlannedBackDown is in beta, so each feature is marked with its status.
Works today

Dedup across everything you own

Dedup across everything you own

Not just inside one repository. Each new drive is checked against everything already indexed. Hardlinks and symlinks are accounted for, so reclaim figures are real.

Works today

Proof a drive is safe to wipe

Proof a drive is safe to wipe

Either every file has a SHA-256-identical copy elsewhere, or you get the list of files that don't. Every copy and deletion is journaled against a verified hash.

Works today

Survives bad hardware

Survives bad hardware

Long jobs pick up where they stopped: hashing, copying and rescues never redo finished work. A drive that drops out mid-scan is scanned again when it's back, and hashing reads one file at a time per file system, so a disk never thrashes.

Works today

A web UI you'll actually open

A web UI you'll actually open

Live progress, interactive size trees, duplicate tables and per-drive verdicts, served locally by the daemon, in light and dark.

Works today

Go back to any scan

Go back to any scan

Every scan is kept, so the file browser can show any folder as it was on any scan date, with previews and read-only viewers for PDFs, office documents, SQLite databases, git history and diffs.

Works today

Knows what things are

Knows what things are

Maildirs, Time Machine sets, phone backups, home directories, disk images, git repos, SQL dumps and cloud exports, each with a date range and size. Regenerable caches are flagged, and can be left out.

Works today

Knows where it came from

Knows where it came from

BackDown reads the rsync scripts, sync markers and backup metadata that record your data's history. It can say "rsynced from your mail server on 31 May 2020," not just "some files."

Works today

Browse without restoring

Browse without restoring

Mailboxes appear as threaded mail, photos as a gallery, SQL dumps as schemas. Disk images open read-only, no mounting needed. Search every backup and drive at once.

Works today

Rescans in seconds

Rescans in seconds

After the first scan, BackDown asks the drive's own change log what's changed: the FSEvents history on macOS or the USN journal on Windows, even after the drive was unplugged. On NTFS drives it can also read the master file table directly, listing millions of files in seconds. Anything the log can't vouch for is scanned in full, so nothing is missed. Free in every edition.

In development

Plugged in once, never forgotten

Plugged in once, never forgotten

Plug in a new drive and BackDown indexes it as soon as it's mounted, without changing anything on it. Unplug it, even halfway through a scan, and its index stays: still searchable, and brought up to date the next time it's back. If it turns up at another path, it's recognised, not indexed twice.

Planned

Scheduled, encrypted backups

Scheduled, encrypted backups

Content-defined chunking, zstd compression and client-side encryption, verified on a schedule, to local disks, SFTP, S3 or B2.

Works today

A chain of custody

A chain of custody

Signed, append-only manifests of every copy, move and delete, a record you can hand to an auditor or a court.

Privacy

Your data stays on your disks.

Most backup services start by uploading everything. BackDown starts from the opposite end.

No network by default

The local edition makes no network requests. It needs no account and sends no telemetry.

Never writes to a source

BackDown never writes to a drive it's analysing, and drives it mounts for you are mounted read-only, so a flaky enclosure can't corrupt the data you're trying to save.

Never deletes without proof

Nothing is removed unless a copy with a matching hash is already in the journal.

Cloud is opt-in

The optional team dashboard sees metadata only. Your files leave your machines only if you add a cloud backup target.
